title: Tulsidas Bows First
hookLine: a husband crosses a flood at night, and his wife sends him to Ram
carry: begin with a bow to Ganesha and Saraswati
tomorrow: Why would a holy poem bow to wicked people?

cards: It's night, and the river is high from the rains. A young man comes home to find his wife gone to her parents' house across the water, and he can't stand to wait until morning.

So he crosses the swollen river in the dark and climbs up to her window. She is not charmed. She's embarrassed, and tells him so, sharply: if you loved Ram the way you love this body of flesh and bone, you'd be free.
The young man goes away and doesn't come back. That's how tradition tells the turning of Tulsidas.

teach.b: Tulsidas became a poet of Ram, and his great work is the Ramcharitmanas, the story of Ram retold in Awadhi, a language people spoke, not the Sanskrit of the older Ramayana.
Like Namdev, Tukaram and Kabir this week, he sings in the language of home. But first he bows.

teach.h: A BOW TO VANI AND VINAYAKA.
teach.b: The poem opens with a short run of Sanskrit verses, and the very first one bows to Vani, the goddess of speech, and to Vinayaka, Ganesha: makers of letters and meanings, of the flavors and meters of verse, and of everything auspicious.
That opening bow has a name: mangalacharan, the auspicious beginning.
It's why so many Hindu beginnings look the same: a puja that opens with Ganesha's name, a wedding card with Ganesha at the top, a new notebook marked Shri Ganeshaya Namah.
Ganesha clears the road; the goddess of speech gives the words.
Before a single word of his own, the poet thanks both. Tulsidas says why he writes: for the happiness of his own heart, svantah sukhaya. Not for fame.
And the poem explains its own name. It says Shiva composed this story first and kept it in his own mind, his manas, so it's called the Manas of Ram's deeds.
A man once turned around by his wife's sharp words begins his life's work with a bow, thanking the givers of words, and passing on a story Shiva held in his heart.

how: Hindus who love Ram read and sing the Ramcharitmanas at home and in temples, sometimes all the way through over several days, and its verses are chanted and staged in Ram Lila performances.

games.why: the poem's first verse bows to Vani and Vinayaka, the mangalacharan, and soon says he writes for his own heart's joy.

practice: Before the next thing you start today, a page, a message, a task, pause for an opening bow. Many Hindus say or write Shri Ganeshaya Namah, a bow to Ganesha, or ask Saraswati for the right words.
Say it softly, or touch the page and ask for a clear road and good words. If you don't pray, name one thing you're grateful for before you begin, and start for the joy of it.

wordCard.voice: Tulsidas. The poet of the Ramcharitmanas, who bowed to Vani and Vinayaka at its door, and wrote the story of Ram for the happiness of his own heart.
